sentences.text: This marine reptile reached lengths of 4 to 5 meters and likely hunted small fish or belemnites in both open water and on the sea floor.
Fossil evidence suggests it possessed a comparatively large head, a trait that distinguishes it from other long-necked relatives.
While it is classified as a long-necked plesiosaur, its neck was relatively shorter than that of some similar species like Elasmosaurus.
A fountain featuring sculptures of this animal was erected in the Swedish town of Bromölla in 1971.
The artist Gunnar Nylund constructed the fountain using approximately 3,000 molded ceramic parts set within reinforced concrete.
Locally in Sweden, plesiosaurs and this specific genus are often called swallow-tailed lizards or swan-neck lizards.
The species Scanisaurus nazarowi was first described in 1911 by Nikolay Bogolyubov based on a single vertebral centrum found near Orenburg, Russia.
Later, Per-Ove Persson provisionally designated Swedish fossils as S. cf. nazarowi, noting they were the same species with a fairly high degree of probability.
In 1996, Persson referred a crushed skull to the genus because associated tooth fragments showed the same striae pattern as teeth referred to S. cf. nazarowi.
Although too crushed for much anatomical detail, this skull is the only cranial fossil referred to Scanisaurus and demonstrates its head was comparatively larger than other dolicodiran plesiosaurs.
Per-Ove Persson concluded that Scanisaurus was the most common plesiosaur in Late Cretaceous Skåne because its vertebrae were far more common than those of other species.
A 2017 study interpreted the animal as an intermediate trophic level predator capable of feeding in both open waters and on the sea floor.
Its sharp, elongated teeth indicate it was used to crush or pierce smaller prey such as small fish or belemnites.
Mosasaur bite marks have been found on plesiosaur bones recovered from the Kristianstad Basin.
Scanisaurus is classified in the order Plesiosauria and family Elasmosauridae, with the genus authority cited as Bogolyubov, 1911.
In 1960, Persson referred both Cimoliasaurus and Scanisaurus to a new family of mesodiran plesiosaurs called Cimoliasauridae.
The genus is typically considered an invalid taxon because it lacks diagnostic features to differentiate it from other elasmosaurids.
Scanisaurus lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Sweden and Russia.
During the Campanian, the Kristianstad Basin was a shallow inland sea with a subtropical to temperate climate.
The genus Scanisaurus is considered of questionable validity due to limited type material and a lack of diagnostic features, though it is still used in practice.
Per-Ove Persson noted that the species remained undefinable because it was based on only a single vertebral centrum, yet he felt confident the Swedish material belonged to it.
